Bring the best of human thought and AI automation together at your work. # Difference between Spearman and Kendall-Tau correlation test. My question is not about the definition of the two rank correlation methods, but it is a more practical question: I have two variables, X and Y, and I calculate the rank correlation coefficient with the two approaches. With the Kendall-tau-b (which accounts for ties) I get tau = 0 and p-value = 1; with Spearman I get rho = -0.13 and p-value = 0.44. Why does Kendall tell me there is exactly no correlation, while Spearman does see a nonzero correlation? ## 1 Answer 1. Spearman's $\rho$ and Kendall's $\tau$ are calculated differently. That is, they have different notions of "correlation". (As does Pearson's $r$.) Thus, they will output different correlation coefficients. I don't see anything surprising about having one type of correlation zero and one nonzero. Here is a fun little dataset with $\rho<0$, $r=0$ and $\tau>0$:. > yy <- c(-0.2,2.5,1,2,3.5,-1). > plot(xx,yy,pch=19). > cor(xx,yy,method="spearman"). > cor(xx,yy,method="kendall"). > cor(xx,yy,method="pearson"). So different measures of correlation will output different results. Your next question probably is which coefficient you should use. I am using R to compute a Spearman correlation between two interval datasets (i.e. wave height and North Atlantic Oscillation Index). First question: Am I right by saying that R transforms my interval data to ranked data and then does the correlation? Second question: I am getting the following warning:. `In cor.test.default(hs, df$V1, method = "spearman") :. Cannot compute exact p-value with ties`. So should I use Kendall correlation instead of Spearman? Or is there an option in R for Spearman correlation that can deal with ties? In this event, the **Kendall tau-b** should be used to calculate the p-value, as it is specifically equipped to handle ties. Suppose a correlation test is run using both Kendall and Spearman statistics. `> cor.test(x, y, method = "kendall", alternative = "greater"). Kendall's rank correlation tau. z = 1.1593, p-value = 0.1232. alternative hypothesis: true tau is greater than 0. In cor.test.default(x, y, method = "kendall", alternative = "greater") :. Cannot compute exact p-value with ties`. `> cor.test(x, y, method = "spearman", alternative = "greater"). Spearman's rank correlation rho. S = 62.521, p-value = 0.09602. In cor.test.default(x, y, method = "spearman", alternative = "greater") :. Cannot compute exact p-value with ties`. In both cases, we get the error message "cannot compute exact p-value with ties". We see that in this scenario, the Kendall statistic is accounting for the fact that ties exist in our data and is calculating the p-value accordingly. Michael Grogan's user avatar.
